sweep_summary: Four title-keyword items for tibe1272: Sprigg 1961 (downloaded from SOAS eprints via the Internet Archive. Firthian vowel-harmony study, no stress statement at all — silent); Gong 2014 SEALS 24 (Old Tibetan;org 429, Bing/DDG blocked; medium priority, secondhand via Lim it reanalyses second-syllable H as stress); Caplow 2016 LTBA (paywalled Benjamins DOI, abstract read: σ2 stress on disyllabic non-verbs and σ1 on verbs in Balti and Rebkong Amdo, reconstructed for Proto-Tibetan; silent on Lhasa synchronic stress; medium); Loewe 2000 (Dante translations, irrelevant Glottolog mis-attachment). Two open first-hand sources already held by the project were read: Lim 2018 (uOttawa PhD, acoustic experiment) concludes Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress (p. 105) and rejects the weight/tone stress accounts — this contradicts the catalog's weight-hedged coding from Goldstein & Nornang 1978 and is the best statement found; Meredith 1990 (MIT PhD, Refugee Standard Tibetan speaker) gives a weight-plus-register rule confined to the first two syllables (refines the catalog: heavy = any coda, tone register counts). new_statements.quote: Based on this experiment, I conclude that there is no evidence to support the proposal that LT has a stress system realized through rhyme duration, pitch, or vocal intensity. These acoustic cues, however, are used to signal prosodic word boundaries and word-final syllables. In short, there is no evidence for overt stress, as one can account for tonal processes by formalizing the low tone as LH rather than invoking a stress-assigned H. It is more economical to analyze LT as a stressless language. In this chapter, I have established that LT has no word stress

new_statements.reading: Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress: an instrumental study of rhyme duration, F0 and intensity in 2-4-syllable words (in carrier sentences, several speakers) finds no culminative word-level prominence; the cues pattern with prosodic-word edges and final syllables. The catalog's weight-hedged coding rests on Goldstein & Nornang's (1978: xv) impressionistic textbook note ('the longer syllable tends to take primary stress'); Lim explicitly reviews and rejects the stress accounts (Meredith 1990, Monich 2011; Meredith's speaker is Kham-native) and argues the Proto-Tibetan σ2 stress survives only as the H tone of the second syllable. Contradicts the catalog: Tibetan (Lhasa) should be flagged as a contested / stressless-candidate record (tone-only), not weight-sensitive.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Tibetan has an empty rule; the existing statement (Lim 2018, instrumental, Lhasa) says Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress. Jäschke (1883, impressionistic, describing the pronunciation of written Tibetan with WT/CT dialect notes) asserts a word accent on the root / latter member of compounds, i.e. a different type (accent present, morphologically placed) from the stressless reading. It is compatible with Lim's remark that prominence cues in Lhasa mark prosodic-word edges and with the Proto-Tibetan second-syllable prominence Lim and Caplow discuss (compound-final accent), but as a claim about synchronic word stress it disagrees with Lim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: 'In such cases' = the postponed monosyllabic particles (§9.2-3) that form one word with a preceding nominal or verbal root: the accent goes to the root, not to the particle; in compounds it generally goes to the second (latter) member. An accented open syllable has a comparatively long vowel in Western Tibetan (Ladak) but is short in Central Tibetan (Lhasa). No position-counting rule; prominence is morphological (root vs. enclitic particle, compound-final).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 20 §14: the indefinite article cig/zhig/shig 'is, of course, always without accent'; p. 33 §50: the conversational language of Central Tibet has 'the accentuated interrogative particle e, immediately before the verb' (a particle that does carry accent). Compounds: accent 'generally' on the latter member, implying exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Jäschke 1883/1954 describes Classical/Written Tibetan pronunciation with explicit dialect notes: WT = Western Tibet (Ladak), CT = Central Tibet (Lhasa); the accent statement is given for both, with only vowel quantity differing. Watters 2002's own data are Dzongkha (Pasakha, West Bengal), Lhomi (Sankhuwa Sabha), Solu Sherpa, Dolpo Tibetan and Mugom Tibetan (Nepal), all separate Glottolog languoids; its Lhasa Tibetan passage is second-hand from Mazaudon 1977. The existing Lim 2018 statement is about Lhasa Tibetan. The archive.org Jäschke item is the 1883 Trübner second edition (prepared by H. Wenzel), which the 1954 Ungar edition reprints.

new_statements.quote: In the Lhasa system, only a monosyllable is distinctive for the four contrastive pitches. The non-initial syllable in polysyllabic words is not contrastive for pitch height (or voice quality) and is always overlaid with a high pitch, regardless of its pitch in isolation or citation form. A syllable which is falling in isolation is also falling when it is the final syllable of a polysyllabic word, otherwise it also loses its contrastiveness for level or falling melody. When a word ends in an unstressed syllable, the penultimate syllable carries the level/falling contrast.

new_statements.relation_note: The paper's own data are Dzongkha (Pasakha), Lhomi, Solu Sherpa, Dolpo and Mugom Tibetan, none of which is tibe1272, so its stress remarks on those languages are not about this language. Its Lhasa section (pp. 32-33, after Mazaudon 1977) is compatible with the existing Lim 2018 statement (tone-only, non-initial syllables high, no culminative stress) and adds the templatic word-tone characterization and the observation that final unstressed (particle) syllables shift the level/falling contrast to the penult. Nothing in it supports a positional word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhasa Tibetan is a word-tone (template) language: the four monosyllabic tones contrast only on the first syllable; non-initial syllables are non-contrastive and high; the level/falling contrast sits on the final syllable, or on the penult when the final syllable is an unstressed one (i.e. a particle). No word-stress placement rule is given for Lhasa; 'unstressed' is used of final grammatical syllables. This is Watters's summary of Mazaudon 1977, not his own Lhasa data.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none for Lhasa. For Lhomi (own data, p. 40): 'When the first syllable is long it attracts stress, or perhaps it is because this syllable is stressed that it is lengthened'; for Dolpo (p. 35) a 'perceived stress on the second syllable' in high register is used as a transcription cue.
new_statements.exceptions: For Lhasa: word-final unstressed syllables shift the level/falling contrast to the penult. Own-data languages: Dolpo/Mugom tone templates (final syllable always high falling), Sherpa word tone, Lhomi/Dzongkha syllable tone.

readall_conflicts: Jäschke (1883, pp. 12-13) asserts a word accent that falls on the root rather than on postponed particles and, in compounds, generally on the latter member; this is an impressionistic 19th-century statement about the pronunciation of written Tibetan with Western/Central dialect notes. The existing statement (Lim 2018, instrumental, Lhasa) finds no word stress at all and treats Lhasa Tibetan as a stressless word-tone language. Watters (2002, pp. 32-33, summarizing Mazaudon 1977) describes Lhasa as a word-tone template system and speaks of word-final 'unstressed' syllables, which presupposes a stressed/unstressed distinction between roots and particles but gives no word-stress position; this is compatible with both Jäschke's root-vs-particle accent and Lim's edge-marking cues. The real disagreement is therefore whether root-vs-particle prominence counts as word stress (Jäschke: yes; Lim: no, it is prosodic-word-edge marking plus H tone on the second syllable). The Tournadre & Dorje manual could not be opened, so its position is unknown.

sources.quote: Based on this experiment, I conclude that there is no evidence to support the proposal that LT has a stress system realized through rhyme duration, pitch, or vocal intensity. These acoustic cues, however, are used to signal prosodic word boundaries and word-final syllables. In short, there is no evidence for overt stress, as one can account for tonal processes by formalizing the low tone as LH rather than invoking a stress-assigned H. It is more economical to analyze LT as a stressless language. In this chapter, I have established that LT has no word stress

sources.note: Instrumental study (duration, F0, intensity across 2-4-syllable words in carrier sentences) plus a phonological review: Lhasa Tibetan has no word stress; earlier stress claims (Meredith 1990; Monich 2011; Denwood 1999; Odden 1979; Tournadre & Dorje 2003) are 'perceived prominence' or reflexes of a Proto-Tibetan stress reinterpreted as tone. §3.1 p. 60 rejects Meredith's weight/register hierarchy as 'not phonologically motivated' and notes his speaker's mother tongue was Kham (kham.pa.tsang), so his data are 'not comparable'.

sources.note: The most systematic formal analysis of (Refugee Standard/Lhasa) Tibetan stress; extends Goldstein & Nornang's disyllable remarks into a weight (any coda, not only V:) x register hierarchy within an initial two-syllable window; would change 'heavy'/'what counts as heavy' and 'edge' fields if the weight reading is.
